title: Chat inference SLO acceptance matrix and benchmark plan
summary: Discovery + POC scoping focused on defining latency and throughput SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), acceptance criteria matrix, and a measurement plan. Agreed on synthetic + production trace benchmarks, cold vs warm cache runs, and next steps to share harness and run 10k request sweep. Customer leaning toward Dedicated pilot if p95/p99 targets met.
topics: bench harness, quantization and batching tradeoffs
timeline and acceptance criteria for pilot
next_steps: Alex to share benchmark harness repo link and cost-model spreadsheet by 2025-02-20
Liam to export 7 days of production trace (anonymized) and upload to shared folder by 2025-02-21
Nina to run baseline synthetic sweep (cold + warm) on Redwood hosted and report p95/p99 by 2025-02-25
Schedule follow-up on 2025-03-03 for results review and pilot decision
action_items: Nina Park | Run synthetic TTFT and TPOT sweep (10k requests, 3 warm runs) | due 2025-02-25
Alex Carter | Share bench harness repo URL + deck + example config | due 2025-02-20
Liam O'Connor | Provide anonymized prod traces (chat sessions) and success criteria doc | due 2025-02-21
Raj Patel | Confirm security checklist and whether VPC-only pilot required | due 2025-02-22
transcript: Meeting header: 2025-02-18 15:30 UTC — Duration: ~52m — Attendees: Alex Carter (Redwood AE), Nina Park (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (VisionGrid), Sofia Reyes (VisionGrid), Raj Patel (VisionGrid)

[00:00] Alex Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Alex, AE at Redwood, and Nina is our solutions engineer. Would love to understand your primary success criteria for a POC — is it latency, cost, reliability, or a mix?

[00:15] Liam O'Connor: Hi, thanks. Main thing for us is predictable latency for chat snippets — customers complain when answers take too long. We also care about sustained throughput on peak, we do a lot of concurrent sessions. So both latency and throughput matter, but the order depends on use-case.
[00:34] Sofia Reyes: For product, we want p95 to be < 300ms for short prompts (<= 64 tokens) and p99 ideally under 600ms. If those are met we can move to a dedicated pilot.

[00:50] Nina Park: Got it. Two quick clarifications on terms — when you say latency are you referring to TTFT, time-to-first-token, or TTFF? We usually work with TTFT as primary SLO for perceived latency. For throughput we measure TPOT — time per output token — but sometimes teams prefer tokens/sec. How do you want to frame it?

[01:08] Raj Patel: We're OK with TTFT and tokens/sec as long as you provide equivalence. Our telemetry currently measures response start time and total tokens emitted, so TTFT + tokens/sec maps cleanly.

[01:25] Alex Carter: Perfect. For the POC we recommend an acceptance matrix across short/med/long prompts and cold vs warm cache. Example targets we often see: short prompts (<=64 tokens) p95 TTFT 150-300ms, p99 350-600ms; medium (65-512) p95 TTFT 400-700ms; TPOT target depends on model size but we can translate to tokens/sec — e.g., 20-60 tps on dedicated for certain quantization. These are ballpark and we'll calibrate with your traces.

[02:02] Liam O'Connor: That ballpark aligns with expectations. Can you explain the measurement plan — synthetic vs replaying actual traces? We want numbers that reflect real patterns including prefix lengths and KV cache hit rates.

[02:20] Nina Park: Yes. Our standard plan — step 1: synthetic sweeps to explore configuration space (batch sizes, kv-cache enabled/disabled, quantized model variants). Step 2: replay anonymized prod traces through the harness to capture real SESSION-level behavior (prefixes, branching). Step 3: run warm vs cold cache comparisons, and run at target concurrency to measure TPOT and request queuing. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 and token-level latency histograms.
[02:50] Sofia Reyes: How many samples do you recommend for p99 to be statistically meaningful?

[02:58] Nina Park: For p99 we like >5k requests per workload bucket. For higher confidence 10k is better — especially since extreme tails can be noisy. So our ask: 10k requests per bucket (short/med/long), run 3 independent iterations for warm-state.
[03:20] Liam O'Connor: OK we'll aim for that. What about cold start behavior? We have some low-volume users that see cold kernel invocations.

[03:30] Alex Carter: We capture cold-start explicitly: first-request-after-idle and then time to stable throughput. Cold runs are useful for host scaling behavior. For Dedicated we can pin a pool to avoid cold starts, but we still measure to show difference.
[03:48] Raj Patel: Security/regulatory qu: we need to know if logs and traces can be kept in our VPC for the pilot. Also SOC2 and SAML are table stakes.

[03:58] Nina Park: Redwood Private supports VPC/on-prem telemetry and we can sign an NDA. For hosted we redact traces; for Dedicated we provide private network options. We'll share our security checklist in the repo.

[04:15] Alex Carter: Back to SLOs — let's draft an acceptance matrix today. Example rows: short/med/long prompt buckets; columns: p95 TTFT, p99 TTFT, TPOT mean, TPOT p95, throughput at 95% utilization, cost per 1k tokens. We'll populate with initial targets and you can adjust. Does that approach work?
[04:37] Sofia Reyes: Yes. We also want to include tail-safety checks — e.g., for p99 we need to ensure no more than 2% of requests exceed a hard cap.
[04:45] Alex Carter: Note taken — we'll add a hard cap column and a rollback/fallback policy if cap exceeded.
[04:52] [05:00] Speaker 1 (interrupt): sorry just wanted to ask about quantization — how much regressed quality should we allow?

[05:10] Nina Park: Good question. We recommend running a small eval set of ~200 labeled prompts (functional tests) for quality regression. If quality drops by more than X% (we can define relative eval metric) we won't accept aggressive int8 unless fallback to fp16 is available. We'll include quality gating in the acceptance criteria.

[05:35] Liam O'Connor: Could you walk through an example measurement? Like we take 10k short prompts from prod traces, we run them with kv-cache disabled and enabled, measure TTFT distribution, and then compare against target?

[05:52] Nina Park: Exactly. Sequence: 1) replay 10k short prompts with original session prefixes; 2) record TTFT, total latency, tokens/sec, and any queueing; 3) run same set under quantized model and record regression; 4) repeat for medium and long buckets. We'll produce histograms and a small dashboard.
[06:18] Raj Patel: About TPOT — do you report time-per-output-token or tokens/second? We need both but prefer tokens/sec in our monitoring stack.

[06:27] Alex Carter: We'll provide both and a conversion table. TPOT (ms/token) is useful for model-level tuning; tokens/sec is useful for capacity planning. We'll include recommended batch sizes per instance type and an estimate of cost per 1k tokens.
[06:45] Sofia Reyes: Timeline question — we need results within two weeks to decide on dedicated pilot. Can Redwood run the synthetic sweep quickly?

[06:53] Nina Park: Yes — synthetic sweep we can run within 3 business days after we get config and traces. The full replay-based benchmark depends on trace handoff, but target two weeks is realistic for 10k x 3 iterations across three buckets.

[07:10] Alex Carter: I'll scope resource needs — if you want a Dedicated pilot we can pre-book a small reserved pool for reproducible runs. That helps reduce noise. We can show Hosted + Dedicated comparison.
[07:25] Liam O'Connor: That would be useful. Also curious about fallback policies — if a heavier model breaches latency SLO do you automatically route to smaller model?

[07:32] Nina Park: We support automatic model fallback policies and routing by cost/latency. For the POC we'll test a fallback from fp16 large model to quantized medium model and observe degradation. We'll include functional and safety checks to decide when fallback is allowed.

[07:52] [08:00] Alex Carter: I'll summarize acceptance criteria we propose: (1) short prompts p95 TTFT <= 300ms, p99 <= 600ms; (2) medium prompts p95 TTFT <= 700ms; (3) TPOT median within 20% of baseline tokens/sec target; (4) quality regression < 3% on eval suite; (5) no more than 2% requests exceed hard cap. Anything to add?
[08:23] Sofia Reyes: Add cost per 1k tokens threshold — if hosted solution costs >20% more than our current infra at projected scale we need a cost mitigation plan.
[08:31] Alex Carter: Will add cost CL. Raj anything else on infra/security?
[08:36] Raj Patel: Just confirmation we'll need an audit log export and KMS integration for the Dedicated pilot.
[08:41] Nina Park: Yes we support KMS/HSM integrations on Private and Dedicated; audit log export is standard. I'll attach our security confluence link in the bench repo.
[08:55] Liam O'Connor: On sampling for p99, is 10k per bucket really necessary? We have limited anonymized traces.

[09:02] Nina Park: If you can only provide smaller sets we can still run but will call out wider confidence intervals. Another option: synthesize traffic by sampling your token-length distribution, which gives more control. We prefer real traces for fidelity though.
[09:20] Alex Carter: Ok I'll put both options in the repo: replay harness instructions + a synth generator that matches your token length percentiles. Link will be in the next steps.
[09:33] Sofia Reyes: Also include a simple dashboard template we can put in Grafana — p95/p99 TTFT by bucket, tokens/sec, error counts, and cost per 1k tokens.
[09:44] Nina Park: Will do. We'll also include a sample Prometheus exporter output so you can plug into your stack.
[09:52] [10:00] Speaker 2: Quick question about edge cases — if the model emits many short tokens vs long unicode tokens does that affect the TPOT metric?
[10:08] Nina Park: Yes tokenization differences can matter. We'll normalize by using the same tokenizer as your production inference path. We'll note any tokenizer mismatch as a caveat.
[10:20] Alex Carter: Any blockers on obtaining traces?
[10:25] Liam O'Connor: We need to scrub PII, but our infra team can export anonymized sessions. I'll coordinate with Raj.
[10:31] Raj Patel: We can do that — expect a sanitized S3 upload to the shared bucket. We'll flag whether sessions have long context windows.

[10:38] Alex Carter: Great. Logistics recap in bullets — I'll share bench harness + deck + cost sheet; Nina will run synthetic sweeps; Liam will provide traces; Raj will confirm security requirements; then we reconvene with results.

[10:52] Sofia Reyes: Sounds good. One last nuance — for user-perceived latency we might want to measure time-to-first-meaningful-token (TTFMT) rather than first byte. Is that something Redwood can instrument?
[11:04] Nina Park: Yes we can instrument TTFMT by adding semantic markers in the eval harness. We'll add that as optional metric.
[11:12] Alex Carter: OK wrapping up — I'll email the repo link and proposed acceptance matrix after the call. Thanks everyone.
[11:20] Liam O'Connor: Thanks. We'll aim to get traces by Friday. Good session.
[11:25] Meeting end
